terms.name: driver_age
terms.rationale: Driver age is one of the most fundamental rating factors in motor insurance. Young drivers (<25) and elderly drivers (>70) exhibit significantly higher claim frequencies and severities due to inexperience and declining reaction times respectively. A non-linear transformation (e.g., spline or banded) is recommended to capture the U-shaped risk curve.

terms.name: vehicle_age
terms.rationale: Vehicle age affects both claim frequency and severity. Older vehicles tend to have lower market values (reducing repair/replacement costs) but may have higher mechanical failure rates. It is a standard and well-accepted rating factor in motor pricing.

terms.name: age_driving_licence
terms.rationale: Years of driving experience (proxied by licence age) is a key predictor of risk independent of driver age. A newly licensed older driver carries higher risk than an experienced driver of the same age. This factor is widely used and regulatorily accepted.

terms.name: vehicle_value
terms.rationale: Vehicle value is a primary driver of claim severity for own-damage and theft coverages. Higher-value vehicles attract larger repair and replacement costs. It is a fundamental and universally accepted rating variable.

terms.name: power_to_weight_ratio
terms.rationale: Power-to-weight ratio is a strong proxy for vehicle performance and driving aggressiveness risk. High-ratio vehicles are associated with higher speeds and more severe accidents. It is actuarially justified and preferred over engine power alone as it normalises for vehicle size.

terms.name: seats
terms.rationale: Number of seats is a proxy for vehicle type (e.g., minivans vs. sports cars) and potential occupancy, affecting both bodily injury exposure and vehicle class risk. It is a standard categorical or ordinal rating factor.

terms.name: theft_premium
terms.rationale: Theft premium is a pre-computed risk score reflecting vehicle theft propensity and geographic theft exposure. Including it as a main effect directly captures theft-related risk loading in the total premium model.

terms.name: policy_type
terms.rationale: Policy type (e.g., third-party only, third-party fire and theft, comprehensive) fundamentally determines the scope of coverage and hence expected claims cost. It is a mandatory rating dimension in any motor pricing model.

terms.name: business_type
terms.rationale: Business type distinguishes personal from commercial use, fleet from individual policies, etc. Commercial and fleet vehicles have different risk profiles (mileage, driver pools, cargo) and this factor is standard in motor pricing.

terms.name: payment_frequency
terms.rationale: Payment frequency (annual vs. monthly) is correlated with policyholder financial stability and retention behaviour. Monthly payers tend to exhibit higher lapse rates and slightly different risk profiles. It also captures instalment loading in premium.

terms.name: bonus_score
terms.rationale: Bonus-malus score (or no-claims discount score) is one of the strongest predictors of future claims, as it encodes historical claims experience. It is a cornerstone of motor pricing across most markets and is highly regulatorily accepted.

terms.name: fuel_type
terms.rationale: Fuel type (petrol, diesel, electric, hybrid) is associated with vehicle performance characteristics, typical usage patterns, and repair cost profiles. Electric vehicles in particular have significantly different repair cost structures. A standard categorical main effect is appropriate.

terms.name: vehicle_brand
terms.rationale: Vehicle brand captures residual risk variation related to build quality, parts availability, repair costs, and brand-specific driver demographics not fully captured by vehicle value or power-to-weight ratio. It is a widely used categorical factor in motor pricing.

terms.name: municipality_type
terms.rationale: Municipality type (urban, suburban, rural) is a key geographic risk factor affecting claim frequency (traffic density, road conditions) and severity (repair cost levels). It is a standard and regulatorily accepted territorial rating variable.

terms.name: circulation_area
terms.rationale: Circulation area provides a broader geographic risk dimension (e.g., region or zone) complementary to municipality type. It captures regional differences in claims environment, legal costs, and weather exposure. Standard in motor pricing.

terms.name: fuel_type:seats
terms.rationale: The strongest interaction in the GBM. Actuarially justified: electric/hybrid vehicles are predominantly available in certain seat configurations (e.g., compact cars vs. electric vans), and the risk profile of, say, a large diesel van differs substantially from a small petrol hatchback in ways not captured by main effects alone. The combination determines vehicle class risk more precisely.
terms.actuary_note: Highest H-statistic (0.458). The interaction is plausible because fuel type and seat count jointly define vehicle segment (e.g., electric SUV vs. petrol city car vs. diesel minibus), each with distinct repair cost and frequency profiles. Recommend validating with one-way lift charts by fuel_type within each seat band.

terms.name: policy_type:bonus_score
terms.rationale: Policy type modulates how bonus score translates into risk. A comprehensive policyholder with a poor bonus score is a very different risk from a third-party-only policyholder with the same score (adverse selection dynamics differ by cover level). This interaction is actuarially well-founded and commonly observed in practice.
terms.actuary_note: Second highest H-statistic (0.358). Strong actuarial rationale: bonus score sensitivity to claims history differs by policy type due to coverage scope and adverse selection. Regulatorily defensible as both variables are standard rating factors. Recommend checking for sufficient exposure in all cells.

terms.name: power_to_weight_ratio:seats
terms.rationale: Power-to-weight ratio and seat count jointly define vehicle type more precisely than either alone. A high power-to-weight, low seat count vehicle is a sports car (high risk); a high power-to-weight, high seat count vehicle is a performance van (different risk profile). The interaction captures these vehicle segment distinctions.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.330. Actuarially justified as the combination of performance metric and vehicle size defines vehicle segment risk. Ensure sufficient data in high power-to-weight, high seat count cells to avoid overfitting.

terms.name: theft_premium:bonus_score
terms.rationale: Theft risk and claims history interact because high-theft-risk vehicles owned by poor-bonus-score drivers represent a compounded risk. The bonus score may also partially reflect past theft claims, creating a multiplicative effect on total premium that is not fully captured by additive main effects.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.313. Actuarially plausible: policyholders with poor bonus scores in high-theft areas represent compounded risk. However, note that theft_premium is itself a pre-computed score, so care is needed to avoid double-counting. Recommend reviewing the construction of theft_premium to confirm independence from bonus_score.

terms.name: policy_type:theft_premium
terms.rationale: Theft premium loading is only relevant for policies that include theft coverage (TPFT and comprehensive). For third-party-only policies, theft premium should have minimal effect. This interaction correctly allows the theft risk loading to vary by policy type, which is actuarially essential.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.312. Strong actuarial justification: theft coverage is only present in certain policy types, so the theft premium should interact with policy type. This is arguably a structural interaction that should be included regardless of H-statistic. Regulatorily very defensible.

terms.name: power_to_weight_ratio:vehicle_brand
terms.rationale: Vehicle brand and power-to-weight ratio interact because the same power-to-weight ratio carries different risk implications across brands (e.g., a high-ratio luxury brand vs. a high-ratio economy brand have different driver demographics and repair costs). This interaction refines the vehicle risk segmentation.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.305. Actuarially justified but implementation complexity is high given the number of brand levels. Consider grouping vehicle brands into risk tiers before implementing this interaction to maintain GLM parsimony and avoid sparse cells.

terms.name: vehicle_brand:seats
terms.rationale: Brand and seat count together define vehicle segment (e.g., a premium brand 7-seater SUV vs. an economy brand 5-seater). Repair costs, parts availability, and driver demographics vary significantly across these combinations. The interaction is actuarially justified for vehicle risk segmentation.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.290. Reasonable actuarial basis but may create many sparse cells when combined with vehicle_brand levels. Recommend brand grouping or using a brand risk index before implementing. Monitor for overfitting.

terms.name: bonus_score:municipality_type
terms.rationale: The predictive power of bonus score may vary by geographic area. In urban areas with higher base frequency, a given bonus score level may correspond to a different absolute risk than in rural areas. This interaction captures geographic modulation of the bonus-malus effect.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.249. Actuarially plausible as claims frequency base rates differ by municipality type, affecting how bonus score translates to risk. Regulatorily defensible. Recommend validating with partial dependence plots stratified by municipality type.

terms.name: municipality_type:circulation_area
terms.rationale: Municipality type and circulation area are both geographic variables that together define the territorial risk more precisely than either alone. An urban municipality in a high-risk circulation area is different from an urban municipality in a low-risk area. This hierarchical geographic interaction is standard in territorial pricing.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.215. Strong actuarial and regulatory justification as geographic risk is inherently hierarchical. This interaction effectively creates a finer territorial grid. Ensure sufficient exposure in all geographic cells.

terms.name: bonus_score:payment_frequency
terms.rationale: Payment frequency is correlated with financial behaviour, and its interaction with bonus score may capture a segment of financially stressed policyholders with poor claims history who pay monthly — a compounded adverse risk profile. This interaction has some actuarial basis though it is less structurally obvious.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.208. The interaction has a plausible behavioural basis (financial stress correlating with both monthly payment and poor bonus score), but it is partially data-driven. Recommend including with caution and monitoring for stability across validation periods. Ensure it does not act as a proxy for a protected characteristic.

terms.name: fuel_type:vehicle_brand
terms.rationale: Fuel type availability varies significantly by brand (e.g., some brands are predominantly electric, others diesel-heavy). The risk profile of a given fuel type within a brand context differs from the population average. This interaction refines vehicle risk segmentation and is actuarially justified.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.205. Actuarially justified for vehicle risk segmentation. Implementation should account for the fact that not all fuel type × brand combinations exist in the portfolio. Sparse cells should be grouped or regularised.

terms.name: vehicle_brand:municipality_type
terms.rationale: Vehicle brand mix varies by geography (urban areas have more premium brands), and the risk implications of a given brand differ by territory (repair network availability, parts costs). This interaction captures geographic variation in brand-related risk.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.177. Actuarially plausible but creates a large number of cells. Recommend brand grouping before implementation. Monitor for data sparsity.

terms.name: policy_type:vehicle_age
terms.rationale: The relationship between vehicle age and premium differs by policy type. For comprehensive cover, older vehicles have lower insured values reducing severity; for third-party cover, vehicle age has less direct impact on severity but may affect frequency. This structural interaction is actuarially justified.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.174. Strong actuarial rationale: the depreciation effect on insured value is only relevant for own-damage covers (comprehensive/TPFT), making this a structurally important interaction. Regulatorily defensible.

terms.name: power_to_weight_ratio:fuel_type
terms.rationale: The risk implications of power-to-weight ratio differ by fuel type. Electric vehicles with high power-to-weight ratios have different acceleration profiles and driver demographics than high-ratio petrol vehicles. This interaction is actuarially relevant as the motor market evolves toward electrification.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.160. Actuarially justified and increasingly important as EV penetration grows. The interaction helps avoid mispricing high-performance EVs relative to equivalent petrol vehicles.

terms.name: power_to_weight_ratio:age_driving_licence
terms.rationale: Inexperienced drivers (low licence age) operating high-performance vehicles represent a well-documented compounded risk. This interaction captures the dangerous combination of limited experience and high vehicle performance, which is a classic actuarial risk factor.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.148. Very strong actuarial justification — the interaction of inexperience and vehicle performance is a well-established risk amplifier. Regulatorily defensible and commonly included in motor pricing models.

terms.name: bonus_score:driver_age
terms.rationale: The predictive power of bonus score varies by driver age. Young drivers have short claims histories so their bonus score is less informative; older drivers with long histories have more credible bonus scores. This interaction allows appropriate weighting of the bonus score by driver age.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.143. Actuarially justified: bonus score credibility increases with driving history length, which correlates with driver age. This interaction is regulatorily defensible as it improves risk discrimination without introducing protected characteristic proxies.

terms.name: theft_premium:driver_age
terms.rationale: Theft risk may interact with driver age as younger drivers tend to own different vehicle types in different areas, and their theft exposure profile differs. Additionally, young drivers may be less security-conscious. The interaction has moderate actuarial support.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.141. Moderate actuarial justification. The interaction is plausible but partially data-driven. Recommend including only if it shows consistent lift in out-of-sample validation. Monitor for stability.

terms.name: seats:circulation_area
terms.rationale: Vehicle type (proxied by seats) and geographic area interact because large vehicles (more seats) in urban circulation areas face different congestion and parking risks than in rural areas. This interaction has a reasonable actuarial basis for frequency risk.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.138. Moderate actuarial justification. The interaction captures urban vs. rural risk differences by vehicle type. Recommend validating with exposure-weighted lift charts.

terms.name: theft_premium:payment_frequency
terms.rationale: Monthly payers in high-theft areas may represent a specific risk segment (e.g., lower-income urban policyholders with higher-theft-risk vehicles). The interaction has some actuarial basis but is partially behavioural.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.132. Partially data-driven. The interaction may act as a socioeconomic proxy. Recommend careful review to ensure it does not indirectly discriminate against protected groups. Include only if actuarial lift is demonstrated in validation and legal review is satisfactory.

terms.name: vehicle_value:vehicle_brand
terms.rationale: Vehicle value and brand interact because the same vehicle value implies different risk profiles across brands (e.g., a mid-value luxury brand vehicle vs. a mid-value economy brand vehicle have different repair cost structures and driver demographics).
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.131. Actuarially justified for severity modelling. However, vehicle value and brand are correlated, so the interaction may be partially redundant. Recommend checking VIF and ensuring the interaction adds genuine lift beyond main effects.

terms.name: vehicle_value:power_to_weight_ratio
terms.rationale: High-value, high-performance vehicles represent a distinct risk segment with elevated severity and frequency. The interaction captures the compounded effect of expensive, powerful vehicles that are costly to repair and more likely to be involved in high-speed incidents.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.130. Actuarially justified for premium vehicle risk segmentation. Ensure the interaction does not create instability in sparse high-value, high-performance cells.

terms.name: payment_frequency:driver_age
terms.rationale: Young drivers are more likely to pay monthly due to cash flow constraints, and this combination may represent a specific risk segment. The interaction captures age-related financial behaviour patterns that affect risk.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.124. Partially behavioural and potentially a socioeconomic proxy. Recommend legal and compliance review to ensure this does not indirectly discriminate. Include only if validated actuarial lift is demonstrated.

terms.name: vehicle_value:bonus_score
terms.rationale: High-value vehicles owned by poor-bonus-score drivers represent a compounded severity and frequency risk. The interaction captures the joint effect of expensive vehicles and poor claims history, which is actuarially relevant for total premium.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.122. Actuarially justified: the combination of high vehicle value and poor claims history is a known high-risk segment. Regulatorily defensible.

terms.name: theft_premium:business_type
terms.rationale: Theft risk varies by business type because commercial vehicles have different theft profiles (e.g., tools and cargo theft for vans) compared to personal vehicles. The interaction allows theft premium to be modulated by the nature of vehicle use.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.122. Actuarially justified: commercial use changes the theft risk profile significantly. Regulatorily defensible.

terms.name: seats:age_driving_licence
terms.rationale: Inexperienced drivers operating larger vehicles (more seats, e.g., minivans) face different risks than inexperienced drivers of small cars. The interaction captures the compounded effect of inexperience and vehicle size on risk.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.121. Moderate actuarial justification. The interaction is plausible but less structurally obvious than power_to_weight_ratio:age_driving_licence. Include if validation confirms lift.

terms.name: vehicle_value:theft_premium
terms.rationale: High-value vehicles in high-theft areas represent a compounded theft risk — both the probability of theft and the cost of replacement are elevated. This interaction is structurally important for theft coverage pricing.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.121. Strong actuarial justification for theft coverage. Note that theft_premium may already incorporate vehicle value to some degree — review the construction of theft_premium to avoid double-counting.

terms.name: policy_type:payment_frequency
terms.rationale: Payment frequency loading and its risk implications may differ by policy type. Comprehensive policyholders paying monthly may represent a different risk segment than third-party-only monthly payers. The interaction has moderate actuarial support.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.116. Partially data-driven. The interaction may reflect commercial pricing structures (instalment loadings varying by policy type) rather than pure risk differentiation. Recommend reviewing whether this is a risk or commercial pricing term.

terms.name: municipality_type:business_type
terms.rationale: Commercial vehicles in urban areas face different risk profiles than commercial vehicles in rural areas (e.g., urban delivery vans vs. rural agricultural vehicles). The interaction captures the joint effect of geography and vehicle use type.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.116. Actuarially justified for commercial vehicle risk segmentation. Regulatorily defensible.

terms.name: bonus_score:age_driving_licence
terms.rationale: Both bonus score and licence age measure driving experience and history, but from different angles. Their interaction captures cases where the two signals diverge (e.g., a long-licensed driver with a poor bonus score — a persistently risky driver) or align (reinforcing risk signals).
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.112. Actuarially justified but note that bonus_score and age_driving_licence are correlated. The interaction may be partially redundant with main effects. Recommend checking for multicollinearity and validating incremental lift.

terms.name: vehicle_value:payment_frequency
terms.rationale: High-value vehicle owners paying monthly may represent a specific financial profile. The interaction has some actuarial basis but is partially behavioural and may act as a socioeconomic proxy.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.111. Partially data-driven and potentially a socioeconomic proxy. Recommend legal review and validation before inclusion. The interaction may reflect commercial instalment loading structures rather than pure risk.

terms.name: driver_age:seats
terms.rationale: Young drivers in large vehicles (more seats) represent a specific risk segment. The interaction captures the compounded effect of age-related inexperience and vehicle size, which affects both frequency and severity.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.111. Moderate actuarial justification. Similar rationale to power_to_weight_ratio:age_driving_licence but weaker. Include if validation confirms incremental lift over existing interactions.

terms.name: theft_premium:power_to_weight_ratio
terms.rationale: High-performance vehicles in high-theft areas may be targeted differently (e.g., joyriding vs. organised theft). The interaction has some actuarial basis but is less structurally obvious.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.110. Borderline actuarial justification. The interaction is plausible but may be partially data-driven. Recommend including only if out-of-sample validation confirms consistent lift. Flag for monitoring.

terms.name: vehicle_value:driver_age
terms.rationale: Young drivers of high-value vehicles represent a well-known high-risk segment (inexperience combined with high-performance/expensive vehicles). The interaction is actuarially justified and commonly included in motor pricing models.
terms.actuary_note: H-statistic 0.109. Strong actuarial justification. Regulatorily defensible as both variables are standard rating factors. Recommend including.
